text: If I had to start investing from zero today, here's exactly how I'd do it.
Now, I'm not a financial advisor.
I'm just sharing what I've learned from my own investing journey.
First, you need an investing app.
Some popular options are Fidelity, Charles Schwab, and Robinhood.
I personally use Robinhood, so that's what I'll show you.
Next, you need to choose your account.
A regular brokerage account gives you more flexibility to access your money, although taxes may apply when you sell investments for a profit.
A Roth IRA is designed for retirement.
Your investments can grow tax-free, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free too.
But there are contribution and withdrawal rules.
Once you've chosen your account, connect your bank and deposit some money.
Now, here's where most beginners get stuck.
What should you actually buy?
Instead of trying to pick the next Apple or NVIDIA, you can start by researching ETFs.
Think of an ETF like a basket holding a bunch of different investments.
For example, I personally own VOO.
It tracks the S&P 500, giving me exposure to around 500 major American companies.
And here's the cool part: You don't need hundreds of dollars to get started.
On Robinhood, you can search VOO, tap Trade, select Buy, and enter just ten dollars.
Review your order, submit it, and now you own a small fraction of that ETF.
But buying your first investment is only the beginning.
You can also turn on dividend reinvestment, so eligible dividends automatically buy more shares.
And from there, focus on consistency.
Whether it's five, ten, or twenty dollars each paycheck, the goal is to build a habit you can maintain.
Just remember, investing involves risk, and your investments can lose value.
Make sure your bills and emergency savings are taken care of first.
